fields.foundation: The Macedonian Empire, which arose in the 4th century BCE, grew out of the ancient kingdom of Macedon in the north of the Greek peninsula. Its rise to pan-Hellenic power began in the reign of Philip II (359–336 BCE), who used diplomacy, military innovation and political consolidation to prepare the kingdom for expansion. Macedon had previously been a peripheral and fragmented kingdom, its upland districts held by semi-independent aristocrats and its borders exposed to Illyrian and Thracian raids and to the interference of the southern Greek city-states. Philip's reforms, including the professionalisation of the army, the creation of the sarissa-armed phalanx and strategic marriages to secure loyalty, enabled the kingdom to overcome internal instability and project power outward. The classical city-states were exhausted after the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) and the inconclusive struggles for hegemony among Sparta and its Peloponnesian League, Athens and Thebes that followed, and this gave Macedon its opening. Victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE and the League of Corinth that followed made Philip master of Greece. His son, Alexander the Great (r. 336–323 BCE), then carried Macedonian authority across Persia and into Egypt and India.
fields.socioeconomy: Macedonian society under Philip and Alexander was stratified, combining a warrior aristocracy with a broad base of farmers, herdsmen and artisans. The king relied on the nobility, many of them raised at court as royal pages, for command and administration. Macedon's economy was predominantly agrarian, with fertile plains yielding cereals and wine, while extensive pasture bred the horses essential to the Companion cavalry. The kingdom's own resources, above all timber for shipbuilding and the gold and silver mines around Mount Pangaion, seized by Philip in the 350s BCE, paid for the economy and for military reform. Alexander's campaigns brought Greece, Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia and parts of Central Asia into a single network of trade and tribute, and the captured Persian royal treasuries released very large quantities of bullion into circulation. Cities such as Alexandria in Egypt grew into major commercial centres, attracting merchants, artisans and scholars. Imperial wealth derived from local production, plunder and the taxation of conquered satrapies. Alexander's silver coinage, struck on the Attic standard at mints across the empire, helped standardise exchange and made commerce between regions easier.
fields.military: The army was the Macedonian Empire's chief instrument of expansion. Philip II's restructuring of the army introduced an infantry phalanx armed with the sarissa, a pike of up to about six metres, which made it strong in defence and attack. The army combined this heavy infantry with versatile cavalry, above all the elite Companion cavalry, capable of rapid manoeuvres that exploited gaps in the enemy line. Alexander refined these methods, crossing into Asia in 334 BCE with an army of some 30,000 to 40,000 infantry and about 5,000 cavalry, supported by engineers, archers and siege equipment. His conquest of the Achaemenid Persian Empire included victories at the Granicus (334 BCE), Issus (333 BCE) and Gaugamela (331 BCE), the sieges of Tyre and Gaza (332 BCE), and the defeat of Porus at the Hydaspes (326 BCE), successes in pitched battle and in siege warfare alike. The army's cohesion, discipline and flexible logistics sustained operations across terrain from Anatolia to the Indus. Military service was also a means of reward and integration: plunder, land grants and appointments reinforced loyalty and spread Macedonian influence throughout the conquered regions.
fields.governance: Macedonian imperial government combined personal monarchy with considerable local autonomy. In Macedon itself, kingship was personal and military, with the king bound to his nobles and army by custom rather than by written constitution. In the conquered lands, Alexander relied on loyal Macedonians and, increasingly, on Persian nobles to govern provinces, largely retaining the existing Achaemenid satrapal system while introducing Greek-style civic institutions in new or refounded cities. Law combined local customary codes with Greek legal practice; Alexander generally emphasised continuity to preserve stability, while issuing decrees to secure loyalty. Satraps answered to the king for order, taxation and levies, though Alexander often entrusted finance and garrisons to separate officers. He founded numerous cities named Alexandria and settled them with Greek and Macedonian veterans, which helped consolidate control and spread Greek culture. A royal secretariat under Eumenes of Cardia kept records of correspondence, tribute and military logistics. This balance of local autonomy and royal oversight allowed Macedon to rule a multi-ethnic empire stretching from Greece to the Indus, but it depended heavily on Alexander's personal leadership, as many local loyalties remained with regional elites rather than a distant monarch.
fields.impact: The Macedonian conquests created the Hellenistic world and changed the culture, economy and politics of western Eurasia. Greek language, art and philosophy spread across Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia and Central Asia, influencing government, literature and science for centuries, and Koine Greek became a common language of administration and commerce. The empire linked Mediterranean, Near Eastern and Indian markets more closely than before. Alexandria, and later successor foundations such as Antioch along with older cities such as Pergamon, became centres of commerce, scholarship and culture. Macedonian conquest ended two centuries of Achaemenid rule but also opened opportunities for local elites to participate in Hellenistic administration. The Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid kingdoms inherited and adapted the Macedonian model, which combined military force, economic control and cultural prestige. The resulting exchanges between Greek and Eastern traditions in art, religion and technology contributed to advances in astronomy, mathematics and medicine, and in the east produced hybrid forms such as Greco-Buddhist art.
fields.decline: The Macedonian Empire fragmented almost immediately after Alexander's death at Babylon in 323 BCE, because there was no clear succession plan and his heirs, his half-brother Philip III Arrhidaeus and his infant son Alexander IV, were weak. His generals, the Diadochi, divided the empire through a series of wars (322–281 BCE), from which came the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt, the Seleucid Empire in Asia and the Antigonid kingdom in Macedon. Contributing factors included the logistical difficulty of governing such large territories, populations resistant to foreign rule and tensions between Greek and local elites. Although regional economies and Hellenistic culture flourished, political unity was never restored. Rivalries among the successor states, Celtic invasions and the rise of Rome and Parthia further eroded their power. Rome defeated the last Antigonid king, Perseus, at Pydna in 168 BCE and made Macedonia a Roman province in 146 BCE, ending independent Macedonian rule.
fields.summary: The Macedonian Empire was brief, but its cultural, military and economic innovations shaped Mediterranean and Near Eastern civilisations for centuries.
fields.teaser: Alexander the Great's eleven-year campaign created one of the largest empires of antiquity and spread Greek culture from Egypt to India.
fields.t0: Philip II turned Macedon from a raided frontier kingdom into the master of Greece with a pike phalanx and Companion cavalry.
fields.t1: Alexander the Great conquered the Achaemenid Empire from Egypt to the Indus, spreading Greek language and cities across Asia.
fields.t2: It split among his generals after 323 BCE, but their kingdoms created the Hellenistic world that Rome later absorbed.
fields.dyk: Philip II's phalanx carried the sarissa, a pike of up to about six metres, letting several ranks present their points to the enemy at once.
